lessons.title: Introduction to Database Design and ER Diagrams
lessons.description: Learn database design principles, entities, attributes, relationships and ER diagrams.
lessons.content:
Database design is the process of organizing data into tables and defining how those tables relate to one another. Good database design reduces duplication, improves consistency and makes applications easier to maintain.

A relational database contains tables. Each table contains rows and columns. A row represents one record, while a column represents an attribute.

Example: A college placement system needs to store students, companies and job applications.

Students(student_id, student_name, email)
Companies(company_id, company_name, location)
Applications(application_id, student_id, company_id, status)

An Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD) visually represents the structure of a database. Its main components are entities, attributes and relationships.

Entity: A real-world object, such as Student or Company.
Attribute: A property of an entity, such as student_name or email.
Relationship: An association between entities, such as Student applies to Company.

Common relationship types are one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many. A student can submit many applications, and a company can receive many applications. The Applications table connects the two entities.

Example SQL:
CREATE TABLE Students (
  student_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  student_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  email VARCHAR(150) UNIQUE
);

A good design starts by identifying requirements, defining entities, selecting keys, mapping relationships and checking for unnecessary duplication.

Practice: Design an ER diagram for a library system containing books, members and borrowing transactions.

lessons.title: Primary Keys, Foreign Keys and Table Relationships
lessons.description: Understand database constraints and how relational tables connect.
lessons.content:
Keys identify records and establish relationships between tables.

Primary Key: A column or combination of columns that uniquely identifies each row. Primary-key values cannot be NULL.

Foreign Key: A column or group of columns referencing a candidate key, usually a primary key, in another table. Foreign keys help enforce referential integrity.

Candidate Key: A minimal set of attributes capable of uniquely identifying a record.

Composite Key: A key formed from two or more columns.

Unique Constraint: Prevents duplicate values according to the database engine's NULL-handling rules.

Example:
CREATE TABLE Departments (
  department_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  department_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE Employees (
  employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  employee_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  department_id INT,
  FOREIGN KEY (department_id)
    REFERENCES Departments(department_id)
);

The Employees.department_id column references Departments.department_id. The database prevents non-NULL foreign-key values from referencing nonexistent departments when the constraint is enforced.

One-to-One: Each record in one table relates to at most one record in another. A UNIQUE foreign key can help enforce this.

One-to-Many: One department can contain many employees.

Many-to-Many: Students can enroll in many courses, and courses can contain many students. A junction table such as Enrollments(student_id, course_id) resolves this relationship.

Example junction table:
CREATE TABLE Enrollments (
  student_id INT NOT NULL,
  course_id INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES Students(student_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (course_id) REFERENCES Courses(course_id)
);

Interview tip: A primary key identifies a row; a foreign key establishes and enforces a relationship.

lessons.title: Functional Dependencies and Database Anomalies
lessons.description: Learn functional dependencies and identify insertion, update and deletion anomalies.
lessons.content:
A functional dependency describes a relationship between attributes in a relation. X -> Y means that whenever two rows agree on X, they must also agree on Y.

Example relation:
StudentCourse(student_id, student_name, course_id, course_name, instructor)

Assume:
student_id -> student_name
course_id -> course_name, instructor
(student_id, course_id) identifies each enrollment.

The combined key determines the remaining attributes, but some attributes depend on only part of that key. This can create redundancy.

Database anomalies are problems caused by poorly structured data.

Insertion Anomaly: A new course cannot be stored unless a student is enrolled, if the table requires a student identifier.

Update Anomaly: Changing an instructor requires updating multiple enrollment rows. Missing one row creates inconsistent information.

Deletion Anomaly: Deleting the last enrollment for a course accidentally removes all stored information about that course.

Normalization reduces these anomalies by organizing attributes into appropriate relations.

A partial dependency occurs when a non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of a candidate key. A transitive dependency can occur when one non-key attribute determines another through an intermediate dependency.

Example decomposition:
Students(student_id, student_name)
Courses(course_id, course_name, instructor)
Enrollments(student_id, course_id)

Now student and course information is stored separately from enrollment relationships.

Interview tip: Functional dependencies describe the meaning of the data, not merely patterns observed in a small sample.

lessons.title: Normalization: First, Second and Third Normal Forms
lessons.content:
Normalization organizes relational tables to reduce redundancy and undesirable dependencies.

First Normal Form (1NF): A table has atomic attribute values for its chosen relational representation, and repeated groups are represented as separate rows or tables.

Poor design:
Students(student_id, student_name, phone_numbers)
Example phone_numbers value: '9876543210, 9123456780'.

Better design:
Students(student_id, student_name)
StudentPhones(student_id, phone_number)

Each phone number is stored separately.

Second Normal Form (2NF): A relation is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key. This eliminates partial dependencies on candidate keys.

Example:
Enrollments(student_id, course_id, student_name, course_name)

If (student_id, course_id) is the only candidate key, student_name depends only on student_id and course_name depends only on course_id. Split the table into Students, Courses and Enrollments.

Third Normal Form (3NF): A relation is in 2NF, and for every nontrivial functional dependency X -> A, either X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute. In common simple examples, 3NF removes transitive dependencies between non-key attributes.

Example:
Employees(employee_id, employee_name, department_id, department_name)

Assume employee_id -> department_id and department_id -> department_name. Store department information separately:
Employees(employee_id, employee_name, department_id)
Departments(department_id, department_name)

Benefits include reduced duplication, improved consistency and easier updates.

Normalization does not automatically make every query faster. More normalized schemas can require additional joins.

Practice: Identify the normal form of a table and explain the dependencies that violate the next normal form.

lessons.title: BCNF, Denormalization and Practical Database Design
lessons.description: Explore Boyce-Codd Normal Form and design trade-offs in real applications.
lessons.content:
Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) is a stronger normalization condition than 3NF. A relation is in BCNF when, for every nontrivial functional dependency X -> Y, X is a superkey.

A relation can satisfy 3NF but fail BCNF when a determinant is not a superkey and the dependent attribute is prime.

Example relation:
Teaching(student, course, instructor)

Assume each instructor teaches exactly one course, while a course may have multiple instructors, and each student has one instructor for each course.

Functional dependencies:
(student, course) -> instructor
instructor -> course

Candidate keys include (student, course) and (student, instructor). Every attribute is prime, so the relation can satisfy 3NF. However, instructor is not a superkey, so instructor -> course violates BCNF.

A possible decomposition is:
InstructorCourses(instructor, course)
StudentInstructors(student, instructor)

When decomposing tables, evaluate lossless joins and whether important functional dependencies remain enforceable without additional constraints.

Denormalization intentionally introduces some redundancy for specific performance or reporting requirements. Examples include materialized summaries or storing precomputed totals. It should be justified by measured workloads and maintained carefully to avoid inconsistent data.

Practical design checklist:
1. Identify entities and business rules.
2. Define primary and candidate keys.
3. Establish foreign-key relationships.
4. Determine functional dependencies.
5. Normalize to an appropriate level.
6. Add useful indexes.
7. Test data integrity and query performance.

Interview tip: Explain both the correctness benefits of normalization and the performance trade-offs of decomposition.

quizzes.question: What is the main purpose of database normalization?
options: Reduce redundancy and improve data integrity
Store every entity in one table
quizzes.explanation: Normalization organizes data to reduce unnecessary duplication and update anomalies.

quizzes.question: Which constraint uniquely identifies each row and does not allow NULL?
quizzes.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies records and cannot contain NULL.

quizzes.question: What does a foreign key primarily enforce?
quizzes.explanation: Foreign keys help ensure references between related tables are valid.

quizzes.question: Which table is commonly used to represent a many-to-many relationship?
quizzes.explanation: A junction table stores associations between two entities.

quizzes.question: What does the functional dependency A -> B mean?
options: A and B must have the same data type
B must be a primary key
quizzes.explanation: Rows agreeing on A must agree on B when A functionally determines B.

quizzes.question: Which normal form primarily eliminates partial dependencies on candidate keys?
quizzes.explanation: 2NF requires non-prime attributes to depend fully on candidate keys.

quizzes.question: Which normal form is commonly associated with eliminating transitive dependencies between non-key attributes?
quizzes.explanation: In common simple schemas, 3NF removes transitive non-key dependencies.

quizzes.question: What condition must hold for a relation to satisfy BCNF?
options: The table must contain exactly one key
Every foreign key must be UNIQUE
Every determinant of a nontrivial functional dependency must be a superkey
quizzes.explanation: BCNF requires each nontrivial functional dependency's determinant to be a superkey.

quizzes.question: Which anomaly occurs when removing one record unintentionally removes unrelated information?
quizzes.explanation: A deletion anomaly happens when deleting a record causes unintended information loss.

quizzes.question: What is denormalization?
options: Intentionally introducing redundancy for a specific design or performance goal
Converting SQL into a programming language
quizzes.explanation: Denormalization may introduce carefully managed redundancy to support particular workloads.

exercises.title: Design a Student and Department Database
exercises.description: Create related tables with primary and foreign keys.
exercises.instructions: Write CREATE TABLE statements for Departments(department_id, department_name) and Students(student_id, student_name, department_id). Set department_id and student_id as primary keys in their respective tables. Add a foreign key from Students.department_id to Departments.department_id. Make student_name mandatory.

exercises.title: Create a Many-to-Many Enrollment Relationship
exercises.description: Model student-course enrollment using a junction table.
exercises.instructions: Create Students(student_id, student_name), Courses(course_id, course_name) and Enrollments(student_id, course_id). Use primary keys on Students and Courses, a composite primary key on Enrollments and foreign keys referencing both parent tables.

exercises.title: Normalize Repeated Phone Numbers
exercises.description: Convert a repeated-value design into a 1NF-friendly relational structure.
exercises.instructions: A Students table currently stores student_id, student_name and a comma-separated phone_numbers field. Write SQL CREATE TABLE statements for Students(student_id, student_name) and StudentPhones(student_id, phone_number). Add appropriate primary and foreign keys so each phone number is stored in a separate row.

exercises.title: Normalize Employee and Department Data
exercises.description: Remove redundant department details from employee records.
exercises.instructions: An Employees table contains employee_id, employee_name, department_id and department_name. Assume department_id uniquely determines department_name. Write CREATE TABLE statements for separate Departments and Employees tables, including primary and foreign keys. Explain which redundancy the decomposition removes.

exercises.title: Normalize a Placement Application Database
exercises.description: Design a relational schema for a placement management system.
exercises.instructions: Design SQL CREATE TABLE statements for Students(student_id, name, email), Companies(company_id, company_name), Opportunities(opportunity_id, company_id, role_title) and Applications(application_id, student_id, opportunity_id, status). Define primary keys, foreign keys, NOT NULL constraints where appropriate and a UNIQUE(student_id, opportunity_id) constraint to prevent duplicate applications to the same opportunity. Briefly explain the relationships and why company data should not be repeated in every application row.
